summary: This note gives an overview of Islam in Central Asia, from its arrival in the early 8th century through the Soviet and Chinese restrictions of the 20th century to present concerns. It describes the dominance of Sunni Hanafi Islam, the distribution of Shia Imami and Ismaili communities across specific regions, and the region's role in producing Islamic scholars and major Muslim empires. It closes by noting that concerns about radicalism and religious freedom persist.
one_line: Overview of Islam in Central Asia, covering its 8th-century arrival, regional sects, scholars and empires, and 20th-century restrictions.
key_facts: Islam in Central Asia has existed since the beginning of Islamic history.
Islam is the most widely practiced religion in Central Asia.
The Hanafi school of thought of Sunnism is the most popular school of Islam in Central Asia.
Shiism of Imami and Ismaili denominations predominates in the Pamir plateau and the western Tian Shan mountains, where the population is almost exclusively Ismaili.
A large minority Shia population lives in the Zarafshan river valley, from Samarkand to Bukhara, where it is almost exclusively Imami.
Islam came to Central Asia in the early part of the 8th century as part of the Muslim conquest of the region.
Many well-known Islamic scientists and philosophers came from Central Asia.
The Timurid Empire and the Mughal Empire are among several major Muslim empires that originated in Central Asia.
In the 20th century, the Soviet Union enacted severe restrictions on religious practice in Soviet Central Asia.
The People's Republic of China enacted severe restrictions on religious practice in Xinjiang in the 20th century.
Concerns about Islamic radicalism and religious freedom in the region persist to this day.
